sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Metztli** ​(*metztli*) — ‌Moon ‌· The ​night ​mirror of ​the ​sun — ​belongs to ‌the ​Nahuatl tradition, ​where ‌it is ​catalogued ‌under the ​domain ‌"Moon". The ​name ​means "Moon"[^1].

​**Metztli** ​is the ​Nahuatl ‌moon — ​the word ‌means ​both 'moon' ‌and ​'month,' so ‌she ​is the ‌sky's ​registrar of ​time. ‌Colonial sources ‌give ‌the moon ​several ​faces: the ‌dimmed twin ​Tecciztecatl, ​the dismembered ‌Coyolxauhqui, ​and Metztli ​herself, ‌the calm ​counting ‌presence over ​night, ​calendar, and ​the ​moist arts ‌of healing.[^2]

‌PuniCodex ​records the ‌canonical ​scholarly spelling ​**Metztli** ‌and serves ‌its ‌temple at ‌[its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/metztli/). The ‌displayed ​form is ​ASCII-equivalent ​— a ‌description computed ​from ​the displayed ​form ‌itself. The ​plain ​ASCII form ​*metztli* ‌contains the ​same ‌letters: no ​recovered ‌diacritics or ​special ‌encoding is ‌claimed. The ​work ​here is ​consistent ​citation, capitalization, ‌provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sections.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in the ​colonial ​alphabetic ​corpus and ​in ​logographic writing ‌in ​the codices; ​the ‌restoration uses ​the ‌normalized ​scholarly orthography. ‌Etymologically ​the name ​means ​"Moon"[^1].

The ​canonical ​spelling **Metztli** ‌matches ​the ‌conventional scholarly ​romanization. ‌The plain ​ASCII ‌form *metztli* ​contains ‌the same ​letters, ​so ‌no lost ‌diacritics ‌or encoding ​transition ​is claimed. ‌The ​editorial work ​is ‌to ​fix one ​reviewed ‌reference spelling, ​preserve ‌capitalization and ​provenance, ​and ​keep the ​original ‌evidence visible. ‌The ​displayed form ‌is ​ASCII-equivalent — ​a ‌description ‌computed from ‌the ‌displayed form ​itself.

sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is **/metztli/** ​— ​Restored ​scholarly ‌form.

Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

- ‌**metztli** — ​The ‌canonical ​restored ‌form Metztli.

​For ​the ​modern speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ​is: Read ‌"Metztli" ​using ‌the reconstructed ​pronunciation ‌above; ​the ‌conventional Latin ​spelling ​adds ‌no diacritic ‌marks.

‌The ​conventional ​spelling "Metztli" ‌is ​already ​written in ‌Latin ​letters; ​the ‌lowercase form ​"metztli" ‌differs ​only ​in capitalization.

​The ​pronunciation ‌given above ‌reconstructs ​the ‌sound ​world in ​which ‌Metztli ‌was invoked. ‌Modern ‌speakers ​should ‌not expect ​exact ​identity ​with ancient ‌phonology; ​the ​reconstruction ​is a ‌scholarly ​compass, ​not a ​performance ‌prescription. ​The ‌reconstructed pronunciation ​of ‌Metztli ​is explained ‌separately ‌from ​its ​conventional Latin ​spelling, ​which ‌adds no ‌diacritic ​marks.

sections.body:
**Metztli** ​is ‌moon. ‌The ​name ​means "Moon" ​and ​belongs ​to ‌the ​nahuatl ​tradition.

### ‌Sacred ​Name

‌The ​restoration Metztli ‌returns ​the ​figure ​to ​scholarly ​recognition.

### ‌Moon

​Central ‌domain: moon.

### ​Living ‌Tradition

​Honored ‌in ​nahuatl ‌myth, ​cult, ​and ‌cultural ‌memory.

### Canonical ‌Restoration

​Preserved ​as ‌a ​flagship ​temple ‌with ​its ​canonical ‌scholarly spelling ​and ‌supporting ​evidence.

​The ​domain ​of ‌moon ‌is ​not ‌a modern ​abstraction; ​it ‌names ‌the ‌sphere ‌of ​influence ‌that ​ancient ​worshippers attributed ​to ‌Metztli. ​Temples, ​texts, ​and ‌iconography ​converge ​on ​this sphere, ‌even ​when ‌local ​manifestations ‌differ. ​The ‌PuniCodex ‌restoration ​Metztli ​restores the ​name ​that ‌governs ‌the ​domain.

sections.body:
The ​stories of ‌Metztli place ‌moon at ​the center ​of a ​living mythological ​world.

### Origins ​(Myth)

Metztli ‌appears in ​nahuatl tradition ​as moon. ‌The name's ​meaning, "Moon", ‌shapes the ​narratives told ‌about this ​figure.

### Worship ​and Memory ​(Cult)

Devotees ​and later ​tradition-keepers preserved ‌Metztli in ​ritual, text, ‌and iconography, ​ensuring the ‌name survived ​into the ‌modern scholarly ​record.

‌The myths ​of Metztli ​survive in ‌fragments, summaries, ‌and later ‌retellings. Each ​version reflects ​the interests ‌of its ​tellers — ​poets, priests, ‌philosophers, and ​scholars. The ​PuniCodex entry ‌does not ​privilege a ‌single version; ​it gathers ​the attestations ​so that ​readers can ‌compare them. ‌The restoration ​Metztli gives ‌the figure ​a stable ​name around ‌which these ‌variants orbit.

sections.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or ​artifact in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is ​yet ​assigned to ‌Metztli ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence ​should ​be read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Nahuatl ​name ‌of ​this ‌type the ​material ‌record ​is ‌expected ​to ​be ‌thin, and ‌the ‌primary ​evidence ​remains ‌the ​textual ​testimony gathered ‌in ​the ​Scholarly ‌Sources ​section.

‌Were ​such ​evidence to ​surface, ​it ‌would ‌take ​recognizable ‌forms: ​votive or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming ‌Metztli, ‌sanctuary ​or ‌cult remains ​tied ​to ​moon ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional attributes ​(name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be weighed ‌against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name before ​entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Metztli's ​deepest lesson ‌is lodged ‌in grammar. ​In Nahuatl ​the same ​word names ​the light ​in the ‌sky and ​the interval ​it measures ‌— moon ​*is* month. ‌The Mexica ​did not ‌divide the ​luminous object ​from the ​time it ​kept; the ​watcher and ‌the clock ​were one ‌being. That ​is a ‌more intimate ​astronomy than ‌ours. We ​have inherited ‌a moon ​that has ​been weighed, ‌mapped, and ‌walked upon, ‌and in ​exchange we ​have mostly ‌lost the ​older moon ​— the ‌one that ​told farmers ​when to ‌plant, ​healers when ‌to steam, ​and midwives ​when the ​month had ​turned.

The ‌restoration of ‌Metztli is ​thus more ‌than a ​spelling: it ​is the ‌return of ‌a word ‌that once ‌made time ​personal. When ‌several contradictory ​myths — ​a dimmed ​rival, a ‌dismembered sister, ​a night-lord's ​burden — ​can all ‌be true ​of the ​same pale ​disk, the ‌culture is ​confessing that ‌the moon ​exceeds any ‌single story. ​Perhaps that ‌is the ‌mark of ​a genuinely ​living sky-myth: ​not that ​it resolves, ‌but that ‌it keeps ​counting.[^1]
